strengths: The paper is well motivated by carefully designed preliminary experiments (Section III.B, Fig. 2) showing that after distribution shift a trained DRL solver still ranks good actions highly but produces imprecise action probabilities; this provides a clear empirical rationale for the pruning/selection decomposition.

The proposed method is sensible and clearly described: decoupling the decision-making into a pruning policy and a selection policy, combined with a two-phase training scheme (MAML-based initialization followed by decoupled finetuning), and finetuning only the selection policy at test time.

The evaluation covers both discrete and continuous environments and both in-distribution and OOD datasets, with ablations (ASAP w/o Decouple, ASAP w/o MAML) that support the contribution of each design component; the comparison against recent SOTA baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) is appropriate.

The paper attacks a practically relevant and under-explored problem (cross-distribution generalization and rapid adaptation for online 3D-BPP), and the empirical identification of the key generalization failure factor is itself a useful contribution.
weaknesses: Multiple broken references ('details in ??', 'see in ??', 'more details in ??') indicate that key supporting material — including the first set of motivation experiments (MCTS with pruned action sets) and dataset details — resides in an apparently missing appendix. This directly undermines the evidential support for the central motivating claim.

Statistical rigor is insufficient: no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and Fig. 2 has no error bars. Many reported adaptation gains are small (0.1–0.9% on in-distribution datasets), so it is unclear how many of these differences are statistically meaningful.

The pruning mechanism is underspecified. The pruned action set is defined as Â_t = {a ~ π^p(a|s_t)}, i.e., via sampling, but the paper never explains how many actions are retained, what threshold or top-k rule is used, or how pruning cardinality affects the type I/type II error trade-off the paper itself introduces. Notation is also confusing since Â_t denotes both the pruned action set and the advantage estimate in Eq. (2).

Presentation and internal consistency problems: the manuscript is in an IEEE/APS-style template rather than the ICML format; reference formatting is incomplete (venue/journal names missing in most entries); Section V.B contains an internally contradictory sentence ('a maximum enhancement of 1.3% and a minimum of 2.1%' — max < min); typos such as '3B-BPP', 'when reas GOPT'.

The claim that adaptation is 'completely overlooked by previous work' is overstated, and the methodological novelty is limited: the approach is essentially a combination of a two-head policy decomposition with standard MAML and finetuning. The claimed advantage that finetuning only the selection policy is faster/more effective (Section I) is asserted but never directly measured (e.g., no adaptation cost/flops/wall-clock comparison against finetuning a single non-decoupled policy under equal budgets).

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, no seeds or number of runs are reported, and important hyperparameter details (pruning threshold, MAML inner/outer step sizes, adaptation learning rate) are either missing or deferred to the missing appendix. There is no limitations or ethics discussion.

Some evidence is asserted rather than shown: e.g., the claim that the pruning policy generalizes better than the selection policy (Section IV.B) is given only as an observation without dedicated experiments, and the 'significantly deviate' claim in Fig. 2(b) is qualitative.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and practically relevant problem: cross-distribution generalization and rapid online adaptation for DRL-based online 3D-BPP solvers, which prior work (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) does not directly target.

The motivating analysis in Section III is a nice touch: the MCTS-based pruning experiment and the Optimal Frequency vs. Policy-Induced Frequency comparison (Fig. 2) provide a plausible empirical justification for decoupling pruning from selection.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: both discrete and continuous environments, four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution subsets, and comparisons against three recent SOTA baselines under a matched training/adaptation protocol.
Ablation study (ASAP w/o Decouple, ASAP w/o MAML) isolates the two proposed components, and ASAP w/o Decouple alone already outperforms baselines, supporting the decoupling claim.
weaknesses: The manuscript is not in a submittable state: multiple broken cross-references render as '??' (Section III.B, Section IV.c, Fig. 2 caption context, dataset details), 'details in ??' for the core constraints, and errors such as 'Table Table I', '3B-BPP', and 'when reas GOPT'. Crucially, several key motivating results are deferred to references that resolve nowhere, so the central empirical motivation is not fully verifiable in the paper.

The core methodological detail of the pruning policy is vague: A_t-hat is defined as {a ~ pi^p(a|s_t)}, i.e., actions are 'pruned' by sampling from a distribution. How many actions are retained, at what threshold, and how this trades off type I vs. type II errors is never specified. This is essential for reproduction and for understanding the method's cost/benefit.

Adaptation gains are small and reported without any uncertainty quantification: improvements of +0.2% to +0.9% utilization on in-distribution datasets, with no error bars, standard deviations, or significance tests across the 64 instances per subset. Several claimed improvements (e.g., GOPT -0.2 on ID-Large) suggest noise-level variation, yet the paper draws strong conclusions from these differences.

The text contains internally contradictory claims that undermine confidence in the results: Section V.C states a 'maximum enhancement of 1.3% and a minimum of 2.1%' (a maximum smaller than the minimum), and other numerical summaries (e.g., '1.9% to 3.0%' continuous gains) are hard to verify against the tables.

Equation (2) trains the pruning policy with a policy-gradient loss on actions a_t sampled by the selection policy; this off-policy update is applied without importance weighting, and the resulting bias is neither acknowledged nor analyzed. The type I/II error framing is introduced but never measured empirically.

The MAML setup is unclear: training instances are stated to be generated from the Default item set, yet Algorithm 1 requires 'a batch of distributions p_i(I)'. How these task distributions are constructed, and whether baselines receive an equally favorable meta-learning setup, is not explained.

Only two ablations are provided. There is no comparison against (i) finetuning a non-decoupled policy with equivalent additional compute, (ii) alternative meta-learning schemes (e.g., Reptile or simply multi-distribution training), or (iii) any analysis of inference-time overhead introduced by the second policy.

During adaptation, all methods finetune on 200 batches drawn from the test distribution; the practical scenario where the test distribution is unknown (the very motivation of the paper) is only partially addressed, and the sensitivity to adaptation-set size is not studied.
No mention of code or data release, and no limitations discussion; given the small margins and the reliance on a specific heuristic-based action generator (PCT), reproducibility is a concern.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper targets both cross-distribution generalization and rapid adaptation for online 3D-BPP, which prior DRL solvers (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) do not explicitly address; the gap is clearly identified.

The core empirical observation (Figure 2: after distribution shift, a DRL solver still ranks good actions highly even though its induced action distribution becomes miscalibrated) is a nice, carefully designed motivation experiment, and it directly justifies the pruning/selection decomposition.

The proposed method is clearly described: decoupling into a pruning policy and a selection policy, a two-phase MAML-based initialization followed by policy-decoupled finetuning, and adaptation of only the selection policy at test time. The type I/type II error framing of the interaction between the two policies is intuitive and helpful.

Extensive evaluation: discrete and continuous environments, four in-distribution subsets, three OOD subsets, comparisons against three recent SOTA baselines under a shared training/adaptation protocol, and two ablations (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple) that isolate the contribution of each component.

The ablation results are informative: ASAP w/o Decouple generalizes well but adapts less, while ASAP w/o MAML adapts strongly, supporting the claim that both components contribute complementary benefits.

Honest and largely reproducible experimental reporting: dataset definitions, container sizes, batch sizes, epoch counts, adaptation-data ratio (1/300 of training items), and evaluation protocol are all specified.
weaknesses: Broken cross-references undermine the central motivation: the key preliminary experiments in Section III.B refer the reader to '??' (both the MCTS pruning comparison and the distribution details), so the evidence supporting the paper's central premise is not actually present in the manuscript. Similarly, the constraints are deferred to '??'. This must be fixed before the claims can be verified.

Statistical rigor is missing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere, yet many headline improvements are small (e.g., adaptation gains of 0.2–0.9% on in-distribution datasets, and some deltas of 0.0–0.3% for baselines). Without variance estimates it is hard to tell whether some of these differences are meaningful.

There are signs of carelessness in the text that erode confidence: '3B-BPP' in the introduction; 'when reas GOPT performs best'; and in Section V.C.b the sentence 'a maximum enhancement of 1.3% and a minimum of 2.1%' is internally contradictory (minimum exceeds maximum) and inconsistent with the table, which reports 1.3–2.1%.

The claimed reasons for faster adaptation via selection-only finetuning (plasticity loss avoidance, smaller action set for exploration) are plausible but not experimentally isolated; no experiment compares finetuning the full solver vs. the selection policy under matched compute, and no wall-clock/rollout budget for MAML training is reported despite MAML being computationally expensive.

The gains of ASAP over its own ablations are modest in absolute terms (often <1% utilization), and in some cells ASAP w/o MAML actually achieves larger adaptation improvements than the full ASAP (e.g., +2.1 vs +1.5 on OOD-Small discrete), which weakens the narrative that both components are always jointly beneficial; this is acknowledged but deserves deeper analysis.

No discussion of limitations, no statement about code release, and no analysis of inference-time cost of the two-policy architecture versus single-policy baselines, which matters for the claimed practical-deployment motivation.

The manuscript is not in the conference's standard format (IEEE/RevTeX style), and the 'maximum (resp. minimum)' phrasing describing gains over baselines conflates generalization and adaptation claims at times; the writing needs a careful pass.

Adaptation is evaluated using finetuning data drawn from the same distribution used to create each test subset; a more realistic evaluation with only partial or noisy knowledge of the test distribution would strengthen the practical relevance of the adaptation claim.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper goes beyond cross-distribution generalization and explicitly targets rapid online adaptation of DRL-based 3D-BPP solvers, a goal genuinely overlooked by prior work (PCT, AR2L, GOPT), as confirmed in the related work discussion.

The preliminary study (Section 3.2, Appendix A.2) using MCTS to approximate optimal action frequencies is a thoughtful empirical analysis; it grounds the design conjecture (promising-action identification generalizes better than optimal-action selection) in data rather than assertion, and Table 3 showing DRL-proposal MCTS nearly matches full MCTS with reduced complexity is convincing supporting evidence.

Comprehensive experimental design: both discrete and continuous environments, four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution dataset subsets, comparison against three recent SOTA baselines, two ablations (w/o Decouple, w/o MAML), sensitivity analysis over k (Tables 6-7), and time-cost breakdowns (Table 5, Figure 9) that also motivate the adaptation objective via simulation cost.

The two-phase (pre-training/post-training) scheme with MAML meta-learning is sensible, and the ablation cleanly attributes gains to both the decoupled architecture and the meta-learning initialization; the conclusion that the two components are complementary is supported by the tables.
Reported inference/training overhead of ASAP is negligible relative to baselines, addressing a practical concern with the two-policy design.
weaknesses: Absolute improvements are modest: generalization gains of roughly 2-3% utilization and adaptation gains of 0.3-2.2% over the best baseline. With only 3 random seeds and no variance estimates or statistical significance tests, it is unclear all reported differences are meaningful, especially the small ID-dataset adaptation deltas (e.g., +0.2/+0.3%).

Confounded comparison with baselines on generalization: ASAP uses MAML-based meta-training while baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT) are trained without it. The ASAP w/o MAML variant partially mitigates this, but the headline comparisons versus baselines conflate the architecture change with the training-scheme change; a MAML-equipped baseline is not provided.

The core 'conjecture' rests on a top-3 inclusion rate of only ~65% on cross-distribution instances (Figure 2b), which is moderate rather than strong evidence; the claim that pruning generalizes 'better' is supported mainly by qualitative curve-shape arguments in Figures 5-7 rather than a quantitative cross-distribution comparison of proposal vs. selection error.

Incremental novelty: decomposing decision-making into candidate generation and selection closely resembles existing practice in 3D-BPP (heuristic-generated candidate placements selected by a DRL policy in PCT-style methods); the contribution is essentially adding a learned, meta-trained pruner on top of this paradigm plus selection-only fine-tuning, which is a natural rather than surprising design.

Presentation issues undermine polish: repeated typos ('3B-BPP', 'decarsing'), Table 4 contains a duplicated row label ('Number of leaf nodes for discrete environment' with values 50 and 100), Figure 2 axis labels are illegible at print size, and several references lack venue names entirely (e.g., Martello et al., Crainic et al.).

The online adaptation protocol fine-tunes on 200 batches drawn from the test distribution itself; the paper does not discuss how realistic this assumption is (availability of labeled test-distribution instances), and it references 'rebuttal material' tables (Tables 3/6/7 framing) that should have been integrated consistently.

No explicit limitations section; limitations are only hinted at in the conclusion, and code/data are only promised 'upon acceptance', limiting immediate reproducibility despite fairly detailed hyperparameters in the appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically motivated problem: rapid adaptation of DRL-based online 3D-BPP policies to new item distributions, which prior work in this specific domain has largely ignored.

The preliminary analysis (Section 3.2, Figures 2, 5-7, Table 3) is a genuine attempt to build an empirical understanding: comparing MCTS-derived 'optimal frequencies' with policy-induced distributions, and measuring top-k inclusion rates, gives an evidence-based motivation for the proposal/selection decomposition.

The experimental protocol is fairly comprehensive: in-distribution and OOD datasets, discrete and continuous environments, three SOTA baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT), ablations (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple), sensitivity to the proposal set size k (Tables 6-7), and time-cost analysis (Tables 1-2, 5, Figure 9).
ASAP consistently outperforms the baselines without adaptation in nearly all settings, and the reported training-time overhead of the two-phase scheme is small (Table 5).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core ingredients are standard and well-established. The proposal-then-selection decomposition is a familiar candidate-generation/pruning idea, and the adaptation mechanism is off-the-shelf MAML applied to a specific domain. The claim that adaptation is 'completely overlooked by previous work' overstates the novelty, as meta-learning for fast adaptation is a mature research area; the contribution is essentially an application of known techniques to 3D-BPP.

The absolute improvements are small and their significance is not established. Gains over the best baseline are often around 1-3%, adaptation improvements are frequently only 0.2-0.9%, and the paper uses only 3 random seeds with no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests reported anywhere. Given these margins, it is unclear whether many differences are meaningful.

The empirical evidence partially contradicts the central claims. In Table 2, ASAP w/o MAML achieves larger adaptation improvements than full ASAP on OOD (+1.9 vs +1.5 discrete; +2.3 vs +2.1 continuous; +1.9 vs +1.3 on OOD-Large continuous), and in Table 1 w/o MAML beats ASAP on ID-Small (+1.4 vs +0.9), undermining the argument that MAML-based initialization is the key to adaptation.

Circularity in the motivation experiments: the 'Approx Optim' and 'Optimal Frequency' baselines come from an MCTS whose rollouts use a DRL policy and whose expansions are pruned by that same DRL policy's top-k proposals (Table 3). The 'optimal' reference is therefore not independent, and the claimed 65%+ top-3 inclusion rate partly reflects the MCTS construction itself.

Internal inconsistencies and careless writing undermine confidence: Section 5.2.2 states 'a maximum enhancement of 1.3% and a minimum of 2.1%' (minimum larger than maximum); '3B-BPP', 'decrasing', 'hyperparemters'; Table 4 lists 'Number of leaf nodes for discrete environment' twice with different values (50 and 100); several references lack venue names; Figures 2 and 7 are illegible at the printed scale. References to 'Table 3 in rebuttal material' and 'Tables 6 and 7 in rebuttal material' (Section A.5) suggest the text was recycled from a rebuttal without careful revision.

The adaptation protocol needs clarification: the policy is fine-tuned on 200 batches (12,800 instances) sampled from the test distributions using simulator access. The paper does not precisely specify what information is available at adaptation time in a real deployment, so the practical realism of the 'online adaptation' setting is unclear, especially given that the resulting gains in many in-distribution settings are under 1%.

The meta-learning task construction is questionable relative to the evaluation: MAML treats sampled distributions as tasks, but these are drawn from the Default item set, whereas the evaluation tasks (ID-Large/Medium/Small, OOD variants) are different item sets. Why within-Default task diversity should yield transfer to genuinely new item sets is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is weak at submission time: no code or data are released ('will be publicly available upon the paper's acceptance'), no seeds for the 100 sampled distributions per subset, and several methodological details (exact MAML inner-loop configuration for the two decoupled policies) are only sketched.

The datasets are synthetic grids of cuboid sizes (e.g., l,w,h ∈ {2,4,6,8,10}); no experiment tests realistic logistics distributions (correlated dimensions, size clusters, heavy tails), limiting evidence for the practical claims about warehouse deployment.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated by a carefully designed diagnostic study (Section 3.2): using MCTS to approximate an optimal policy and comparing Optimal vs. Policy-Induced frequencies gives empirical grounding for the proposal/selection decomposition, and Figure 7/Table 3 support the claim that ranking promising actions generalizes better than selecting the optimal one.

The proposed design cleanly connects the diagnosis to the method: fixing the proposal policy and fine-tuning only the selection policy at test time is a natural and practical adaptation strategy given a limited learning budget.

The evaluation is quite comprehensive: both discrete and continuous environments, four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution subsets, comparisons against three strong SOTA baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT), ablations (w/o Decouple, w/o MAML), sensitivity to the proposal set size k (Tables 6-7), and detailed time-cost analyses (Table 5, Figure 9) that justify the practical value of adaptation versus retraining from scratch.
Reproducibility support is reasonable: hyperparameters (Table 4), dataset construction details, hardware, seed count (3), and a commitment to release code and data.

The time-cost analysis (Figure 9) convincingly argues why online adaptation matters in this domain, since simulation dominates the cost of training from scratch (6-7 days) versus 22 minutes of adaptation.
weaknesses: The headline improvements are modest in absolute terms: ASAP gains roughly 1-3% utilization over the best baseline, and adaptation gains are frequently below 1%. With only 3 random seeds and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals reported anywhere, it is hard to judge how reliable these small margins are.

The core 'key conjecture' rests on an approximate optimality proxy that is partly circular: MCTS rollouts use a well-trained DRL policy for simulation, so the 'Optimal Frequency' is biased toward the behavior of the very policy class being diagnosed. The claim that 'identifying promising actions is less distribution-dependent than selecting optimal actions' is thus supported empirically but not established rigorously, and only on a small family of synthetic item distributions.

Methodological novelty is incremental: the ingredients (heuristic-generated candidate actions, GAT policy, ACKTR, MAML, top-k pruning, two-phase training) are all existing techniques recombined for this problem. The contribution is a sensible architecture/training recipe for online 3D-BPP rather than a new technique with broader applicability; the promised extension to other decision-making scenarios is left as future work.

The reliance on the PCT/EMS heuristic pipeline constrains scope: all candidate actions come from a fixed heuristic generator, so ASAP inherits its candidate-quality bottleneck, and the method remains limited to cuboid items in a single fixed-size container. Experiments with alternative heuristics (EV, EP, CP) are mentioned but not shown.

The adaptation protocol raises deployment-realism questions that are not fully addressed: online fine-tuning requires environment interaction with reward signals (i.e., simulator access) on the new distribution; the paper does not discuss whether such simulator access is realistic in the motivating logistics scenario, nor how performance degrades if the adaptation budget or the distribution drift magnitude varies.

Signs of hasty writing: '3B-BPP' typo (p.1), text such as 'maximum enhancement of 1.3% and a minimum of 2.1%' (Section 5.2.2, numbers reversed), references to 'Table 3 in rebuttal material' and 'Table 6 and Table 7 in rebuttal material' (Appendix A.5) indicating unpolished integration of rebuttal content, and reference entries missing venue/journal names.

GOPT is not evaluated in the continuous environment (marked '/'), so the continuous comparisons involve one fewer baseline, and it is unclear whether GOPT could trivially be extended; additionally, no alternative adaptation baselines (e.g., simply training with distribution augmentation, or meta-RL variants beyond MAML) are compared under the same adaptation budget.
